meta.title: Who really said "Your true home is in the here and the now"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Thích Nhất Hạnh almost certainly wrote it. Wikiquote sources the line to his 2006 essay “Returning Home” — but that magazine page is now offline.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Your true home is in the here and the now'?
meta.ogDescription: Wikiquote sources this line to Thích Nhất Hạnh’s 2006 essay “Returning Home.” The magazine page is gone, so we mark it attributed, not verified.

answer.label: Attributed to
answer.authorDates: 1926–2022 · Vietnamese Thiền Buddhist monk, peace activist and author
answer.sourceLine: Credibly credited to Thích Nhất Hạnh, and squarely his central teaching on dwelling in the present moment. Wikiquote’s sourced section traces this exact wording to his essay “Returning Home” in Shambhala Sun (March 2006). We could not read that essay — the cited address is dead and no copy was reachable — so the citation stands on Wikiquote rather than on the page it points to.

source.heading: The source

docMeta.dd: Not readable — the cited shambhalasun.com address no longer resolves
The sentence opens a longer paragraph that continues “Your true home is not an abstract idea…”

source.excerpt: Your true home is in the here and the now. It is not limited by time, space, nationality, or race. Your true home is not an abstract idea. It is something you can touch and live in every moment. With mindfulness and concentration, the energies of the Buddha, you can find your true home in the full relaxation of your mind and body in the present moment. No one can take it away from you.
trail: Wikiquote’s page for Thích Nhất Hạnh ↗ carries this sentence in its sourced quotes, with the citation “Returning Home,” Shambhala Sun (March 2006). We fetched the page source and confirmed the wording and the citation sit together.

That citation’s link is dead. The host shambhalasun.com no longer resolves at all, and neither a live successor copy nor an archived snapshot could be reached from here, so the essay itself remains unread. We are recording that gap rather than presenting the citation as checked.

Your True Home: The Everyday Wisdom of Thich Nhat Hanh ↗ is catalogued at the Internet Archive as a Shambhala collection of 365 daily teachings (Boston, 2011, ISBN 9781590309261, with Melvin McLeod as associated editor). Its title repeats this phrase, which is an observation about the phrase’s standing in his work, not a page citation — we could not search inside the book.
Wikipedia ↗ confirms his life dates and that he founded the Plum Village tradition of engaged Buddhism.
source.excerptNote: This is the passage as Wikiquote prints it, not as we read it in Shambhala Sun. The quotable first sentence is almost always lifted out of this longer paragraph.

author.name: Thích Nhất Hạnh
author.heading: About Thích Nhất Hạnh
author.metaLine: 1926–2022 · Vietnamese Thiền Buddhist monk, poet and peace activist
author.bio: Thích Nhất Hạnh — born Nguyễn Xuân Bảo in Huế, Vietnam, in 1926 — was a Thiền Buddhist monk, poet and peace activist who became one of the most widely read Buddhist writers in the English language. Exiled from South Vietnam in 1966 for refusing to take a side in the war, he was nominated for the Nobel Peace Prize by Martin Luther King, Jr. the following year, founded the Plum Village monastery in southwest France in 1982, and is credited with coining the term “engaged Buddhism.” His gift was rendering Buddhist teaching in plain, warm English — which is why a line like this one travels so far from the page it was printed on.

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: Thích Nhất Hạnh spent most of his adult life unable to go home: exiled from Vietnam for campaigning to end the war, he was refused re-entry for decades. Read against that, the line is not a soft piece of mindfulness advice but a claim made under pressure — that a home which can be taken from you by a border was never the real one.

The paragraph it comes from makes the political edge explicit. It ends by saying that others can occupy your country and even imprison you, but they cannot take away your true home and your freedom. The quotable first sentence is usually clipped off from that.
detailsBody: The phrase became a kind of shorthand for his teaching. Shambhala published a 365-day collection titled Your True Home in 2011, and the sentence circulated widely again after his death in 2022.

Our caution here is narrow and specific. There is no sign the line is misattributed, and nothing we found contradicts it; what we could not do is read the magazine essay Wikiquote cites, because the page is gone from the web. That is the whole distance between “attributed” and “verified” on this record.
context.pull: A home a border can revoke was never the real one.

sourcesVerified.claim: Wikiquote’s sourced section carries “Your true home is in the here and the now. It is not limited by time, space, nationality, or race.” and cites it to “Returning Home,” Shambhala Sun (March 2006).
Thích Nhất Hạnh lived 11 October 1926 to 22 January 2022 and founded the Plum Village tradition of engaged Buddhism.
Shambhala published Your True Home: The Everyday Wisdom of Thich Nhat Hanh (Boston, 2011), ISBN 9781590309261, 365 daily teachings, Melvin McLeod as associated name.
Going Home: Jesus and Buddha as Brothers (2000) by Thích Nhất Hạnh is catalogued at the Internet Archive.
The URL Wikiquote cites for “Returning Home” is dead — the host shambhalasun.com does not resolve, so the essay could not be read and the primary remains unverified.
